note: Owner decisions recorded 2026-11-17: 32 approved, 2 rejected (SolarWinds, too generic). Approved lines are copied into sales-notes.json as roleNotes. Round 2 (2026-11-17): proposedRevision on 7 CISO lines approved by the owner on 2026-11-17 and applied to sales-notes.json.

notes.note: Shows how far trust in one vendor's updates can reach; third-party software is a board-level risk.
Vendor updates run with broad access, so deciding which updates to trust is an operations question too.
A dependency that spreads itself makes package intake and install scripts part of the attack surface.
Dev and CI tokens on build machines are exactly what this kind of attack goes after.
A vendor's script ran inside customers' pipelines, so anything those pipelines could read was in reach.
One leaked build credential reached into other companies' CI; build-time secrets need the same care as code.
Pinning Actions by tag wasn't enough; a tag can be repointed after you trust it.
Secrets printed into build logs are a leak path many teams don't watch.
Malicious packages now use the developer's own AI tools to search the machine for secrets.
Tokens and SSH keys sitting on developer laptops are the prize; how long they stay valid matters.
One engineer's laptop led to every customer being told to rotate secrets; a vendor's incident becomes your rotation project.
Rotating every secret stored in a CI platform at once is the real cost; you need to know where they all are.
The missed credentials were ones believed unused; the gap was knowing what each credential could still open.
notes.proposedRevision: An incomplete credential list turned a vendor's breach into an intrusion at Cloudflare itself.
notes.revisionReason: Names the consequence (a second incident) instead of a principle.

notes.note: Service tokens and service accounts outlive the projects that made them; rotation needs a complete list.
A key in a private repo is still exposed the moment someone gets into the repo.
An AWS key in code turned access to a code repository into access to cloud data.
A single signing key was enough to forge access; key custody is a top-level risk.
notes.proposedRevision: One acquired key was enough to forge access to email accounts. Expect your board to ask who controls keys like that.
notes.revisionReason: Replaces 'key custody is a top-level risk' with what the board will actually ask.

notes.note: Keys that mint tokens need the tightest custody; where they live and who can reach them matters most.
Secrets can hide in build outputs like compiled files, not just in source code.
Public container images can carry credentials left over from the build that made them.
A share token scoped to a whole storage account turned sharing a few files into a much larger exposure.
Research and data-sharing repos need the same secrets review as production code.
Cloud keys in exposed web app config files were the starting point for an extortion campaign.
Deployment config files holding live keys are something attackers scan the internet for.
A vendor's support system held session tokens; what you send to vendors is part of your exposure.
notes.proposedRevision: Files your team uploads to a vendor's support desk can carry live session tokens. Vendor support is part of your attack surface.
notes.revisionReason: Makes it about something the CISO's own team does.

notes.note: Troubleshooting files like HAR files can carry live session tokens; scrub them before they leave.
A contractor's public code held a live server key; third-party developers' repos are your exposure too.
A key left public by a contractor can stay public for years; contractor code needs the same checks as yours.
notes.proposedRevision: A contractor's mistake left customer records at risk for almost five years. Their code is your liability too.
notes.revisionReason: Leads with the business impact and duration from the reviewed headline.

notes.note: A bought password plus repeated MFA prompts got past two-factor; identity hygiene is a top-level risk.
notes.proposedRevision: Two-factor gave way to a bought password and repeated push requests. Push-only MFA is worth raising with leadership.
notes.revisionReason: Replaces 'identity hygiene' with a specific control to bring up.

notes.note: Once inside, the attacker reached other employees' accounts with elevated permissions; internal access scope matters.
AI tooling let one tracked actor run operations across many organizations at once; the scale is what's new.
notes.proposedRevision: One tracked actor used AI tooling to work through many organizations at once, so expect attempts in volume.
notes.revisionReason: Turns 'the scale is what's new' into what it means for the CISO.

notes.note: Automated attack agents work through internet-facing weaknesses at volume; external exposure is the first place to look.
The incident became public through an SEC filing; disclosure and recovery planning are board topics.
notes.proposedRevision: West had to report this in an SEC filing. For public companies, incident disclosure is now part of the CISO's job.
notes.revisionReason: Ties the incident to a responsibility the CISO owns.

notes.note: Encrypted systems disrupted operations worldwide; recovery time is the operational question.
